rounds.text: Supreme Facility Management Ltd is currently trading at a significant disconnect from its fundamental performance, evidenced by a P/E ratio of 4.2x [E1] and a price-to-book ratio of 0.52x [E2], both of which sit well below their respective sector benchmarks [E6, E7]. This valuation is particularly striking given the company’s robust growth trajectory, highlighted by a 62% compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months [E19] and a 23% compounded sales growth over the last five years [E14]. The market appears to be pricing in a contraction, as the reverse DCF suggests the current price implies an earnings growth of -9.1% [E41], which stands in stark contrast to the company's actual accelerating results [E56]. Furthermore, the intrinsic value derived from a discounted cash flow model sits at Rs 148 per share, offering a substantial margin of safety of 85.4% against the current market price [E39, E40]. Conceded: the company carries leverage risk with a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.50x [E31], reports negative free cash flow [E30], and provides no dividend yield to shareholders [E4, E47]. Despite these headwinds, the strong commitment from promoters, who hold 71.52% of the company [E35], combined with increasing domestic institutional interest [E37], suggests that the current market sentiment may be failing to account for the underlying operational momentum [E56].

The bull’s reliance on low valuation multiples [E1, E2] ignores the severe liquidity and solvency risks that likely justify such a discount. While the bull cites profit growth [E19], it fails to reconcile this with a massive negative free cash flow of Rs -36 Cr [E30], suggesting that reported profits are not translating into actual cash generation. Conceded: the company has delivered good profit growth [E46]. However, this growth is overshadowed by a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.50x [E31] and rising borrowings of Rs 154 Cr [E33], which create a precarious financial position that is further strained by a low interest coverage ratio [E48]. The bull’s optimism regarding institutional interest is contradicted by the fact that overall institutional money flow is negative [E38] and foreign institutional holdings have been completely liquidated [E36]. Finally, the reliance on a DCF model [E39] is speculative when the company fails to pay any dividends [E4, E47] and exhibits inconsistent operating margins [E26, E27], indicating that the business model lacks the stability required to support the bull's high valuation assumptions.
